Title: Trust Infrastructures Virtual Asset Service Providers
Text:
Trust Infrastructures for Virtual Asset Service Providers
(Extended Abstract)
Thomas Hardjono
MIT Connection Science & Engineering
Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Cambridge, MA 02139, USA
hardjono@mit.edu
September 9, 2020
Abstract
Virtual aset service providers (VASPs) curently face a number of chalenges, both
from the technological and the regulatory perspectives. In the context of virtual aset
transfers one key isue is the ned for VASPs to securely exchange customer information
to comply to the Travel Rule. We discus a VASP
information sharing network as one
form of a trust infrastructure for VASP-to-VASP interactions. Related to this is the ned
for a trusted identity infrastructure for VASPs that would permit other entities to quickly
ascertain the legal busines status of a VASP. For regulated walets, an atestation infras-
tructure may provide VASPs and insurance providers with beter visibility into the state
of walets based on trusted hardware. Finaly, for customers of VASPs there is a ned
for seamles integration betwen the VASP services with the existing consumer identity
management infrastructure, providing a user-friendly experience for transfering virtual
asets to other users.
Keywords: Virtual Asets, Blockchains, Trust, Infrastructure

Introduction
It has ben over a decade since the advent of the Bitcoin cryptocurency system [1] based on
the hash-chain model of Haber and Storneta [2]. Considerable interest, hype and speculative
investments have gone into various projects on blockchains aimed at developing decentralized
virtual aset ecosystems. At the same time, there has ben a growing trend of theft and mis-
apropriation of virtual asets [3, 4]. Aditionaly, crypto-curencies are stil being exploited
for money-laundering [5, 6], raising signiﬁcant concern on the part of regulators.
The FATF Recomendation No. 15 [7] that was ﬁnalized in mid-2019 provided an unam-
biguous deﬁnition of virtual asets and virtual aset service providers (VASP). This places
VASPs under much of the same AML-related regulations as that of traditional ﬁnancial in-
stitutions, notably the Travel Rule. In short, the Travel Rule requires a VASP to obtain,
validate and retain their customer’s personal information ned for compliance. In the case
of virtual aset transfers betwen an originator and a beneﬁciary, their coresponding VASPs
must share per-wise the customer information pertaining to the originator and beneﬁciary.
Today many users posesing virtual asets (e.g. cryptocurencies) expect aset transfers
through VASPs to be conﬁrmed or setled in a mater of seconds. However, the ned for
VASPs to exchange and validate customer information prior to aset transfers may impose
delays on the setlement of transfers. Furthermore, VASPs do not as yet have an agred
mechanism to exchange their respective customer information in a secure and reliable maner.
We believe that this lack of an information exchange mechanism points to a more funda-
mental chalenge facing the VASP comunity worldwide: namely the lack of
trust infrastruc-
tures that are highly scalable and interoperable, which permit busines-trust and legal-trust
to be established for per-to-per transactions of virtual asets acros diﬀerent jurisdictions.
There are several forms of trust infrastructures neded for VASPs, and in the curent
work we discus thre forms or types of such infrastructures. The ﬁrst is an
information
sharing infrastructure speciﬁcaly for VASPs.
The main purpose of a VASP information
sharing infrastructure is to securely and conﬁdentialy share customer information related
to transfers of virtual asets. Related to this network is the VASP
identity infrastructure
that permits VASPs and other entities to quickly ascertain the busines legal status of other
VASPs. Next is an
attestation infrastructure that can suport VASPs and aset insurers
in obtaining beter visibility into the state of customer walets based on trusted hardware.
Finaly, there is a ned for a
claims infrastructure for customer data sources that integrates
seamlesly into the existing user digital identity infrastructure.
2
The Travel Rule and VASP Customer Information
With the emergence of blockchain technologies, virtual asets and cryptocurencies, the FATF
recognized the ned to adequately mitigate the money laundering (ML) and terorist ﬁnanc-
ing (TF) risks asociated with virtual aset activities.
The
Financial Action Task Force
(FATF) is an inter-governmental body established in 1989 by the ministers of its member
3


countries or jurisdictions. The objectives of the FATF are to set standards and promote
eﬀective implementation of legal, regulatory and operational measures for combating money
laundering, terorist ﬁnancing and other related threats to the integrity of the international
ﬁnancial system.
The FATF Recomendation 15 [7, 8] deﬁnes a
virtual asset as a digital representation of
value that can be digitaly traded, or transfered, and can be used for payment or investment
purposes. Virtual asets do not include digital representations of ﬁat curencies, securities and
other ﬁnancial asets that are already covered elsewhere in the FATF Recomendations. The
FATF deﬁnes a
virtual asset service provider (VASP) to be any natural or legal person who is
not covered elsewhere under the Recomendations, and as a busines conducts one or more
of the folowing activities or operations for or on behalf of another natural or legal person:
(i) exchange betwen virtual asets and ﬁat curencies; (i) exchange betwen one or more
forms of virtual asets; (i) transfer of virtual asets; (iv) safekeping and/or administration
of virtual asets or instruments enabling control over virtual asets; and (v) participation in
and provision of ﬁnancial services related to an isuer’s oﬀer and/or sale of a virtual aset.
The implication of the Recomendation 15, among others, is that VASPs must be able to
share the originator and beneﬁciary information for virtual aset transactions. This proces
– also known as the
Travel Rule – originates from under the US Bank Secrecy Act (BSA
- 31 USC 531 - 530), which mandates that ﬁnancial institutions deliver certain types of
information to the next ﬁnancial institution when a funds transmital event involves more
than one ﬁnancial institution. This customer information includes (i) originator’s name; (i)
originator’s acount number (e.g. at the Originating-VASP); (i) originator’s geographical
adres, or national identity number, or customer identiﬁcation number (or date and place
of birth); (iv) beneﬁciary’s name; (v) beneﬁciary acount number (e.g. at the Beneﬁciary-
VASP).
It is important to emphasize that a VASP as a busines entity must be able to respond
comprehensively to legitimate inquiries from law enforcement regarding one or more of its
customers owning virtual asets (e.g. legal SAR inquiries/warants). More speciﬁcaly, both
the Originator-VASP and Beneﬁciary-VASP must poses the complete and acurate
actual
personal information (i.e. data) regarding their acount holders (i.e. customer). This ned
for actual data, therefore, precludes the use of advanced cryptographic techniques that aim to
prevent disclosure while yielding implied knowledge, such as those based on Zero-Knowledge
Prof (ZKP) schemes [9].
Although beyond the scope for the curent work, one of the key chalenging isues related
to the Travel Rule is the privacy of customer information once it has ben delivered betwen
VASPs. This problem can be acute when one VASP is located within a jurisdiction with
strong privacy regulations (e.g. EU with GDPR [10]), while the other is located in a jurisdic-
tion with an incompatible privacy regulations [1]. More speciﬁcaly, if a Beneﬁciary-VASP
is located under a diﬀerent legal jurisdiction (e.g. foreign country) observing weaker privacy
regulations than the originator’s jurisdiction, there are no means for the originator to ensure
her customer information is not leaked or stolen from that Beneﬁciary-VASP.
4


3
Information Sharing Infrastructure for VASPs
A core part of an information sharing infrastructure is a network shared among VASPs to
exchange information about themselves and their customers. The notion of an
out-of-band
(oﬀ-chain) network for VASPs to share information about themselves and their customers
was ﬁrst proposed in [12] as part of the broader discusion within the FATF Private Sector
Consultative Forum leading up to the ﬁnalization of Recomendation 15 in mid-2019. The
idea of an information sharing network is not new, and the banking comunity established
a similar network (i.e. the SWIFT network [13]) over two decades ago. Today this network
is the backbone for global corespondent banking.
As such, similar to banking data networks, a “network” is neded for VASPs to securely
exchange information about themselves and about their customers for Travel Rule compliance
and other requirements. This information sharing network should be layered atop the proven
TCP/IP Internet, in order to provide the best conection resilience and sped.
There are several fundamental requirements for an information sharing network for VASPs
(Figure 1):
• Security, reliability and conﬁdentiality of transport: The VASP information sharing
network must provide security, reliability and conﬁdentiality of comunications be-
twen an Originator-VASP and Beneﬁciary-VASP. Several standards exists to fulﬁl this
requirement (e.g. IPsec VPNs [14], TLS secure chanels [15], etc.).
• Strong end-point identiﬁcation and authentication: VASPs must use strong endpoint
identiﬁcation and authentication mechanisms to ensure source and destination authen-
ticity and to prevent (reduce) man-in-the-midle types of atacks. Mechanisms such as
X.509 certiﬁcates [16, 17] have ben used for over two decades acros various industries,
government and defense as a practical means to achieve this goal [12].
• Correlation of customer information with on-chain transactions: There must be a mech-
anism to permit a VASP to acurately corelate (match) betwen customer information
(exchanged within the VASP information sharing network) and the blockchain transac-
tions belonging to the respective customers. This must be true also in the case of
batch
transactions performed by a VASP (e.g. in the comingled acounts busines model).
• Consent from originator and beneﬁciary for customer information exchange: Unam-
biguous consent [10] must be obtained by VASPs from their customers with regards
to the transmital of customer personal information to another VASP. Explicit consent
must also be obtained from the beneﬁciary for receiving aset transfers from an origi-
nator. That is, a Beneﬁciary-VASP must obtain consent from its customer to receive
aset transfers into the customer’s acount.
Eﬀorts are curently underway to begin adresing the ned for a VASP information sharing
network to suport VASPs in complying to the various aspects of the Travel Rule (se [18, 19]).
A standard customer information model has recently ben developed [20] that would alow
VASPs to interoperate with each other with semantic consistency.

A Trusted Identity Infrastructure for VASPs
Another part of the information sharing infrastructure is a VASP
trusted identity infrastruc-
ture that permits VASPs to prove their identity, public-key(s), and legal busines information.
A trusted identity infrastructure must adres the various chalenges around VASP iden-
tities and provide the folowing types of mechanism:
• Discovery of VASP identity and veriﬁcation of business status: Mechanism are neded
to permit any entity on the Internet to ascertain whether a virtual aset service provider
is a regulated VASP within a given jurisdiction. An Originator-VASP must be able to
easily locate the identity information for Beneﬁciary-VASP and to rapidly determine
the busines and legal status of that Beneﬁciary-VASP (vice versa).
• Discovery and veriﬁcation of VASP public-keys: Mechanism are neded to permit any
entity on the Internet to ascertain whether a given public-key legaly belongs to (oper-
ated by) a given VASP.
• Discovery and veriﬁcation of VASP service endpoints: Mechanisms are neded to permit
a VASP to ascertain whether it is conecting to the legitimate service endpoints (e.g.
URI) of another VASP (and not a rogue endpoint belonging to an atacker).
• Discovery of VASPs using customer identiﬁers: Mechanisms are neded to permit a
VASP to search and discover a binding (asociation) betwen a customer user-friendly
identiﬁer (e.g. email adres) and the VASP (one or more) that may hold an acount
for that customer.

4.1
Extended Validation Certiﬁcates for VASPs Business Identity
The problem of discovering and verifying service provider public-keys and service endpoints
was faced by numerous online merchants nearly two decades ago. For the end-user (i.e. home
consumer) it was increasingly diﬃcult to distinguish betwen a legitimate service provider
(e.g. online merchant) from rogue web-servers that mimic the lok-and-fel of legitimate
merchants. In response to a growing trend of man-in-the-midle atacks, a number of browser
vendors established an aliance in the late 20s – caled the
CA/Browser Forum (CAB
Forum) – that brought together browser vendors and X.509 certiﬁcation authorities (CA). The
CAB forum, as an industry standards deﬁning organization, published a number of industry
technical speciﬁcations refered to as
Extended Validation (EV) identity certiﬁcates [21].
The overal goal was to enhance the basic X.509 certiﬁcate [16, 17] with aditional busines
related information regarding the subject (i.e. the online merchant). The CA that isues EV-
certiﬁcates must perform the various information background checks regarding the subject,
to ensure that the subject was a legitimate busines. Corespondingly, the browser vendors
suported EV-certiﬁcates by pre-instaling a copy of the rot CA certiﬁcate of al compliant
CAs into their browser software.
We believe a similar aproach is suitable for fulﬁling a number of the VASP requirements
discused above. Some of the subject (VASP) busines information to be included in the
VASP identity EV-certiﬁcate could be as folows [18]:
• Organization name: The Organization ﬁeld must contain the ful legal name of the
VASP legal entity controling the VASP service endpoint, as listed in the oﬃcial records
in the VASP’s jurisdiction.
• VASP Alternative Name Extension: The Domain Name(s) owned or controled by the
VASP and to be asociated with the VASP’s server as the endpoint asociated with the
certiﬁcate.
• VASP Incorporation Number or LEI (if available): This ﬁeld must contain the unique
Incorporation Number asigned by the Incorporating Agency in the jurisdiction of in-
corporation. If an LEI number [2] is available, then the LEI number should be used
instead.
• VASP Address of Place of Business: This is the adres of the physical location of the
VASP’s Place of Busines.
• VASP Jurisdiction of Incorporation or Registration: This ﬁeld contain information
regarding the Incorporating Agency or Registration Agency.
• VASP Number: This is the globaly unique VASP number, if used (se OpenVASP [19]).
• VASP Regulated Business Activity: Curently, no formal deﬁnition of busines activity
speciﬁc for VASPs have ben deﬁned. Note that in reality VASPs may operate diﬀerent
functions in the virtual asets ecosystem (e.g. crypto-exchanges, virtual aset based
fund managers, stablecoin isuers, etc.).
7


• EV Certiﬁcate Policy Object Identiﬁer: This is the identiﬁer for the policies that deter-
mine the certiﬁcate procesing rules. Such policies could be created by the organization
using the certiﬁcate, such a consortium of VASPs (se section 4.3 below).
4.2
VASP Transactions-signing and Claims-signing Certiﬁcates
For asets in comingled acounts managed by a VASP, the aset transfer on the blockchain is
performed by the VASP using its own private-public key pair on behalf of the customer. The
customer holds no keys in the comingled cases. We refer to these private-public keys as the
VASP
transactions signing-keys, and we refer to coresponding certiﬁcate as the
transactions
signing-key certiﬁcates. The purpose of signing-key certiﬁcates is to certify the ownership of
the private-public keys as belonging to the VASP. A given VASP may own multiple transac-
tions signing-keys and therefore multiple signing-key certiﬁcates.
Because a VASP must stand behind the customer information it provides to other VASPs,
any
claims [23] or
assertions [24] that a VASP produces about its customers must be digitaly
signed by the VASP. We refer to these private-public keys as
claims signing-keys, and we refer
to coresponding certiﬁcate as the
claims signing-key certiﬁcates.
It is crucial for a VASP that these thre (3) key-pairs be distinct. This is because the key-
usage purpose of the keys are diﬀerent, and each key may have diﬀering lifetime durations.
Depending on the proﬁle of a transactions signing-key certiﬁcate and the claims signing-key
certiﬁcate, they may include the serial number (or hash) of the identity EV-certiﬁcate of the
VASP. This provides a mechanism for a recipient to validate that the owner of these two
certiﬁcates is the same legal entity as the owner of the VASP identity EV-certiﬁcate.
4.3
Consortium-based VASP Certiﬁcate Hierarchy
In order for VASPs to have a high degre of interoperability – at both the technical and
legal levels – a
consortium arangement provides a number of advantages for the informa-
tion sharing network. Members in a consortium are fre to colectively deﬁne the comon
operating rules that members must abide by. The operating rules become input mater into
the deﬁnition of the
legal trust framework which expreses the contractual obligations of the
members.
A wel-crafted set of operating rules for a VASP information sharing network provides its
members with the several beneﬁts. First, it provides a means for the members to
improve
risk management because the operating rules wil alow members to quantify and manage
risks inherent in participating within the network. Secondly, the operating rules provides its
members with
legal certainty and predictability by adresing the legal rights, responsibilities,
and liabilities of participating within the network.
Thirdly, the operating rules provides
transparency to the members of the network by having al members agre to the same terms
of membership (i.e.
contract).
Since the operating rules is a legal contract, it is legaly
enforceable upon al members. Finaly, a set of operating rules which deﬁne comon technical
speciﬁcations (e.g.
APIs, cryptographic functions, certiﬁcates, etc.), for al the members
8


Figure 2: Overview of a certiﬁcate hierarchy for VASP consortium
provides the highest chance of technical interoperability of services. In turn, this reduces
overal system-development costs by alowing entities to re-use implementations of those
standardized technical speciﬁcations. Several examples of consortium-based operating rules
exist today (e.g. NACHA [25], OIX [26]).
Using the identity EV-certiﬁcates mentioned above as an example, the comon operating
rules would deﬁne the technical speciﬁcation (proﬁle) of the EV-certiﬁcate (e.g. cryptographic
algorithms, key lengths, duration of validity, isuance protocols, revocation protocols, etc.),
as wel as the legal information that must be included in the EV ﬁelds of the certiﬁcate (e.g.
legal incorporation number, LEI number, place of busines, etc.).
Busines interoperability can only be achieved if al members of the information shar-
ing network observe and implement these comon operating rules, and if there is legal and
monetary liability for not doing so. This aproach is not new and is used for group per-
ing agrements among IP routing service providers (i.e. aces ISPs and backbone ISPs).
Technological interoperability of identity EV-certiﬁcates dictates that members of the infor-
mation sharing network participate under a comon
certiﬁcate hierarchy, that is roted at
the consortium organization. This is shown in Figure 2, where the consortium becomes the
Rot-CA for the certiﬁcates isued to al VASPs in the consortium organization.
Certiﬁcate hierarchies have ben sucesfuly deployed in numerous organizations, rang-
ing from government organizations [27], to ﬁnancial networks [13], to mobile devices and
networks [28], to consortiums of cable-device manufacturers [29]. An example of a consor-
tium that brings together device manufacturers (i.e. Cable Modem and Set Top Box vendors)
and service operators (i.e. regional cable aces providers) is Cable Laboratories (CableLabs).
The combined type of membership in CableLabs permits cable operators to detect and iso-

This combined aproach may be relevant for VASPs dealing with customer walet devices.
5
Customer Identity and Key Management Infrastructure
There is today a ned for crypto-aset management systems to be integrated seamlesly
with existing identity management infrastructure functions, including identity authentication
services, authorization services, and consent management services.
5.1
Customer Identities and Digital Identiﬁers
Curently most users employ their email adres as a form of user
identiﬁer in the context
of obtaining services on the Internet. Many of these identiﬁers do not represent the user’s
ful person (core) identity [30], and have short-term or ephemeral value (i.e. identiﬁer can be
replaced with a new one). Typicaly the entities who isues the identiﬁers are email providers
and social media platform providers.
The industry jargon used to describe them (rather
inacurately) is
Identity Provider (IdP). Besides providing email-routable identiﬁers to users,
the identity provider’s role in the identity ecosystem is to provide mediated authentication
services and credential-management on behalf of the user [31]. Mediated authentication –
such as single sign-on (SO) – provides convenience for the user by obviating the ned for them
to authenticate multiple times to each online service provider (e.g. online merchant) they
visit. The online merchants redirects the user temporarily to the IdP for user-authentication,
and upon suces the user is returned back to the merchant.
The predominance of email-identiﬁers for users is a mater of consideration for VASPs
10


because some users may wish to use their email adres as the main identiﬁer for acount-
creation at the VASP. They may also sek to use the email identiﬁer of a beneﬁciary in the
context of aset transfers. Furthermore, a user may have multiple acounts, each at diﬀerent
VASPs and each employing diﬀerent email identiﬁers obtained from diﬀerent IdPs.
An interesting aproach is used in the PayID scheme [32] where the user is identiﬁed using
a string similar to the
addr-spec identiﬁer (RFC532), but with the “@” symbol replaced by
the dolar sign (“
$”) while retaining the local-part and the domain-part. For example, if
Alice has an acount at the PayID provider (e.g. ACMEpay.com) then her PayID identiﬁer
would be
alice$acmepay.com.
5.2
Identiﬁer Resolvers
The mater of user identiﬁers is important not only from the customer usability perspective,
but also from the ned for interoperability of services acros VASPs within the information
sharing network.
When an Originator-VASP employs a user-identiﬁer scheme to identify
an originator and beneﬁciary, then the Beneﬁciary-VASP must have the same syntactic and
semantic understanding of the identiﬁer scheme. That is, both VASPs must be identifying the
same pair of originator and beneﬁciary customers. Thus, another use of the VASP information
sharing infrastructure discused previously is for VASPs to exchange the list of identiﬁers of
their respective customers. This can be achieved by each VASP in the network employing
an
Identiﬁer Resolver Service (server) that is acesible to other VASPs in the network (se
Figure 3).
Some of the general requirements for a VASP resolver service are as folows (non-exhaustive):
• Support for multiple user-identiﬁers: The resolver service must permit multiple types
of user-identiﬁers to be asociated with the customer of the VASP.
• Fast lookup for VASP determination: The resolver service must suport fast lok-ups
or searches based on an identiﬁer string by other VASPs in the network. Such lok-ups
may be part of an aset-transfer request from a VASP’s customer and any delays in
identifying the Beneﬁciary-VASP may ad to the overal transfer setlement time as
perceived by the customer.
• Protected service APIs: The service endpoint APIs (e.g. RESTful, PubSub, etc.) of
the resolver service must be protected.
A caler VASP must be authenticated and
authorized to use the APIs.
• Validation of user-identiﬁer to IdP: Optionaly, for every user-identiﬁer string submited
(aded to) by a customer to their acount at the VASP, the resolver service of the
VASP should validate the string to its original isuer (if it was not the VASP). Thus, if
customer Alice wishes to employ her email adres
alice@idp1.com then the resolver
service should sek to validate that Alice is known to the provider IdP1.
Figure 3 ilustrates that both Alice and Bob can be recognized using thre diﬀerent
means: (i) their email adres isued by an IdP (e.g.
alice@idp1.com); (i) their PayID
1


adres managed by a VASP (e.g.
alice$ovasp.com); or (i) their bare public-keys (e.g.
alice-pubkey).
Using Figure 3, consider the example of Alice who wishes to transfer virtual asets to
Bob, but who only knows Bob’s email adres (e.g.
bob@idp2.com). Alice does not know
Bob’s public-key or Bob’s VASP. This means that Alice’s Originator-VASP must query its
resolver service – as shown in Step 2(a) and Step 2(b) of Figure 3 – to discover which other
VASPs in the network may know of the string
bob@idp2.com (i.e.
uses the string in an
acount). Asuming the resolver service returns a positive response (i.e. VASP-identiﬁer or
VASP-number found), the Originator-VASP can begin inquiring to that VASP about Bob
per the Travel Rule, as sumarized in Step 3 and Step 4 of Figure 3.
Note that the resolver service of the Originator-VASP may return more than one posible
Beneﬁciary VASP-identiﬁer or VASP-number.
This could mean that Bob has an active
acount at each of these VASPs (each posibly using a diﬀerent private-public key pair). In
such cases, the Originator-VASP may ned to request further information (regarding Bob)
from Alice.
It is worth noting that that identiﬁer resolvers are not new, and several resolver protocols
have ben standardized and have ben in wide deployment for over two decades now (e.g.
Domain Name Service (RFC1035), Handle System (RFC3650), etc.). As such, the nascent
VASP industry should consider using and extending these wel-deployed systems, instead of
designing something from scratch.
5.3
Customer Privacy and Resolving to Public-Keys
In general we believe that a VASP resolver service should not return customer public-keys in
the ﬁrst instance in order to preserve customer privacy.
The purpose of the VASP resolver service is to aid other VASPs in determining whether
an entity (person or organization) is a customer of one (or more) of the VASPs in the network.
That is, the resolver service is aimed at solving the VASP
discoverability problem: namely to
lok-up VASP identiﬁers (VASP-numbers) in order to engage that VASP.
Secondly, the information (metadata) about the asociation betwen a user-identiﬁer and
a VASP is les revealing than the asociation betwen a user-identiﬁer and a public-key. As we
mentioned before, user-identiﬁers (e.g. email adreses) asociated with a customer acount
at VASP can be changed by the customer at anytime without impacting the virtual asets
bound to the customer’s public-key. In contrast, a change to the customer’s public-key is
visible on the blockchain system.
Finaly, diﬀerent VASPs may employ diﬀerent busines models (e.g. key-custodian, com-
mingled funds (acounts-only), regulated customer walets). As such, in some cases (com-
mingled funds) there is in fact no unique public-key asociated with a given customer.
12


5.4
Federation of Resolvers: VASP Information Sharing Network
In order for VASP resolver services to scale-up, the VASPs must
federate their resolver services
under a comon legal framework (i.e. the consortium model discused above). A federation
agrement alows VASPs to share customer identiﬁer information (as known to the VASP)
over the information sharing network (discused in Section 3). Inded, this is one of the main
purposes of the network.
For example, using the information sharing network, VASPs can regularly (e.g. overnight)
exchange knowledge about each other’s customer identiﬁers. This is shown in Figure 3 in
Step (a) and Step (b) that runs betwen the VASP resolver services.
Although the precise protocol is beyond the scope of the curent work, in the simplest
form the exchange of customer identiﬁer information betwen VASP resolver services can
consists of pairs of VASP-identiﬁer value and customer-identiﬁer values (i.e. list of customer-
identiﬁers as known to the VASP):
VASP-identifier, Customer-id-1, Customer-id-2, . . . Customer-id-N
This aproach is akin to IP route Link State Advertisements (LSA) used within some link-
state routing protocols (e.g. OSPF (RFC2328). In this case, a VASP is “advertising” its
knowledge of customers bearing the stated identiﬁers.
The exchange of customer identiﬁer information betwen two VASP resolver services
must be conducted through a SL/TLS secure chanel established using the VASP X.509
EV-certiﬁcates to ensure traﬃc conﬁdentiality and source authenticity.
5.5
Customer Managed Access to Claims
In some cases, static atributes regarding a customer (e.g. age, state of residence, driving
license, etc) can be obtained from authorized entities (e.g. government departments) in the
form of aserted claims in one format or another [24, 23], with a ﬁxed validity period. Within
the identity industry, entities which isue signed asertions or claims are refered to as the
Claims Provider (CP). A given customer of a VASP may already be in posesion of a signed
claim (e.g. driving license number) from an authoritative CP (e.g. Department of Motorized
Vehicles), where the claim signature is stil valid. The customer may kep a copy of the signed
claim in the customer’s personal
Claims Store (e.g. mobile device, home server, cloud storage,
etc.). The customer could provide its VASP with a copy of the claims, or the customer may
provide its VASP with aces to the customer’s claims store.
There are several requirements and chalenges for VASP aces to claims store managed
by the customer:
• Customer-managed authorization to access claims-store: Aces to the customer’s claims-
store must be customer driven, where aces policies (rules) are determined by the
customer as the claims owner.
• Notice and consent from customer to use speciﬁc claims: The customer as the claims
owner must determine via aces policies (i) which claims are acesible (readable) to
13


Figure 4: Overview of originator authorization for VASP to retrieve claims
the VASP, (i) the usage-purpose limitations of the claims, (i) and the right for the
customer to retract (withdraw) the consent [10]. The customer’s claims store must
provide notice to the VASP, and the VASP must agre to the terms of use.
• Consent-receipt issuance to VASP: The customer’s claims-store must isue a
consent-
receipt [3] to the VASP which acts exculpatory evidence covering the VASP.
An extension to the OAuth2.0 framework [34] caled the
User Managed Access (UMA) proto-
col [35, 36] can be the basis for customer-managed aces to the claims store. In the example
of Figure 4, the Originator-VASP is seking to obtain signed claims regarding the origina-
tor customer (Alice) located in her claims store. Aces polices have ben set by Alice in
Step (a). In Step 1 Alice provides her VASP with the location of this service provider. When
the VASP reaches the UMA Service Provider (Step 2) – which acts as the authorization server
in the OAuth2.0 and UMA context – the VASP is provided with authorization-token that
identiﬁes the speciﬁc claims the VASP is authorized to fetch (Step 3). The VASP wields the
authorization-token to the claims-store (Step 4). The VASP obtains aces to the relevant
claims and is provided with a consent-receipt by the claims-store (Step 5).
A claim-store can be implemented in several ways. For example, it can be a Resource
Server under the control of the CP, it can reside on Alice’s own mobile device, it can be
placed in a cloud-based Trusted Execution Environment (TE) [37], or it may implemented
in a decentralized ﬁle system such as IPFS/Filecoin [38] based on a decentralized identiﬁer
(DID) scheme [39].
14


6
Attestations Infrastructures for Regulated Wallets
With the increase in the number of individuals and organizations holding private-public
keys bound to virtual asets on a blockchain, there is an increased risk of the los and/or
theft of private-keys. VASPs who are custodians of a customer’s private-public keys and
VASPs who employ their own keys to transact on behalf of customers face the problem of
key management. As such, the use of
electronic wallets based on
trusted hardware – such as
the Trusted Platform Module (TPM) chip [40] – that oﬀers key-protection may increasingly
become a necesity for VASPs for their own busines survival. Funds insurance providers [41]
may sek to obtain evidence of the use of trusted hardware by VASPs and their customers.
This brings to the foreground the chalenge of establishing an
attestation infrastructure for
VASPs that asists them in obtaining greater visibility into the state of walets implemented
using trusted hardware.
In the folowing we use the term
regulated wallet to denote a walet system (hardware and
software) that is in posesion of a customer of a supervised (regulated) VASP [42, 43]. We
use the term
private wallet to denote a walet system belonging to an
unveriﬁed entity [1].
In some cases a VASP may decline to perform an aset-transfer to a public-key thought to
be controled by a walet simply because the walet-holder information is unatainable by a
VASP, despite the VASP querying other VASPs in the information sharing network.
6.1
Attestation Information Relevant to VASPs & Asset Insurers
We use the term
attestation to mean the capability in some trusted hardware to provide prof
that a device (platform) using the trusted hardware can be trusted to corectly and truthfuly
report the internal state of the device [4]. The information reported is signed by the trusted
hardware using an internal private-key that is non-readable by external entities and
non-
migrateable (i.e. canot be extracted) from the trusted hardware. Thus, the recipient (e.g. a
veriﬁer) of the evidence obtains asurance that the signed report came from a particular device
with the speciﬁc trusted hardware [45, 46]. These features provides interesting capabilities
for VASPs in adresing some of their key management chalenges, as wel as AML/FT
compliance neds.
For VASPs and aset insurance providers, there are several types of
attestation evidence
information that can be obtained from a walet regarding keys used to sign aset-related
transactions on the blockchain. The type of atestation evidence is dependent on the speciﬁc
type trusted hardware but generaly consists of the folowing [47]:
• Key creation evidence: The trusted hardware used in a walet must have the capability
to provide evidence regarding the origin of cryptographic keys held by the hardware.
More speciﬁcaly, it must be able to atest as to whether it generated a private-public
key-pair internaly or whether the key-pair was imported from outside.
• Key-movability evidence: The trusted hardware used in a walet must have the capabil-
ity to provide evidence as to whether a private-key is migrateable or non-migrateable [48].
15


This evidence permits the VASP to perform risk-evaluation regarding the posibility
that the walet holder (i.e. its customer) has dishonestly exported a copy of private-key
to another walet (and then use the key-pair in an unregulated maner).
• Wallet system stack evidence: The trusted hardware used in a walet should have the
capability to provide evidence of the software stack present in the walet [45, 46].
A given VASP may demand that customers use only aproved walets based on suitable
trusted hardware. The VASP may also demand customers to create and use new key-pairs
in the trusted hardware for al transactions (i.e. from the time the user becomes a legal
customer of the VASP). This strategy provides the VASP with a clear line of responsibility
and acountability under the Travel Rule with regards to customer-originated transactions.
The VASP has exculpatory evidence regarding the on-boarding of the new customer and the
start of use of the new key-pair.
Virtual aset insurance providers (e.g. crypto-funds insurers) must have the ability to
directly query walets in order to obtain signed atestation evidence from the trusted hardware
in the walets. This gives funds-insurance providers with visibility regarding the robustnes
of the key management lifecycle employed by the VASPs for their regulated walets, and
provides them with tangible information upon which to make their risk-asesment.
6.2
On-Boarding and Oﬀ-Boarding Customers
There are a number of chalenges related to the on-boarding of a customer already posesing
a walet.
In the case that the customer walet is regulated and previously known to an-
other regulated VASP, then there are some practical considerations that the
acquiring VASP
neds to adres. These include: (i) validating whether prior to on-boarding the walet was
regulated or private; (i) validating that the keys present within the walet coresponds to
the customer’s historical transactions (conﬁrmed on the blockchain); (i) verifying whether
a backup/migration of the walet has ocured in the past; (iv) determining whether the
customer’s asets should be moved to new keys, and if so, how the “old” keys wil be treated;
and so on.
The case of a customer leaving a VASP (i.e. oﬀ-boarding) also introduces a number of
questions that may be relevant under the Travel Rule. The
releasing VASP may ned to
adres the folowing: (i) preparing evidence that the walet was in a regulated state whilst
the owner of the walet was a customer of the VASP; (i) whether the customer’s asets should
be moved to a temporary set of keys, denoting the end of the VASP’s responsibilities for the
customer under the Travel Rule; (i) obtaining evidence from the walet that the “old” keys
(non-migrateable keys) have ben erased from the walet device, thereby rendering the keys
unusable in the future by the customer; and so on.
16


7
Conclusions
The VASP information sharing network is a core component of the trust infrastructures
neded if blockchain systems and virtual asets are to be the foundation of the future global
digital economy. VASPs ned to view this information sharing network as a foundational
building block for other infrastructures to be developed.
VASPs also require a trusted identity infrastructure that alow VASPs to authenticate
each other and to rapidly ascertain the busines legal status of other VASPs. The use of
extended-validation digital certiﬁcates oﬀers a promising solution to this problem, based on
wel understod and widely deployed public key certiﬁcates management technologies.
Finaly, other trust infrastructures wil be neded in order to adres use-cases related
to customer walets and device atestations from walets. In particular, VASPs may ned
evidence that the customer’s private-key truly resides within the walet device. This provides
a means for VASPs to prove that they are not the legal operator of the customer’s private-
public keys.

Abstract: ) Thomas Hardjono MIT Connection Science & Engineering Massachusetts Institute of Technology Cambridge, MA 02139, USA hardjono@mit.edu September 9, 2020 Abstract Virtual aset service providers (VASPs) curently face a number of chalenges, both from the technological and the regulatory perspectives. In the context of virtual aset transfers one key isue is the ned for VASPs to securely exchange customer information to comply to the Travel Rule. We discus a VASP information sharing network as one form of a trust infrastructure for VASP-to-VASP interactions. Related to this is the ned for a trusted identity infrastructure for VASPs that would permit other entities to quickly ascertain the legal busines status of a VASP. For regulated walets, an atestation infras- tructure may provide VASPs and insurance providers with beter visibility into the state of walets based on trusted hardware. Finaly, for customers of VASPs there is a ned for seamles integration betwen the VASP services with the existing consumer identity management infrastructure, providing a user-friendly experience for transfering virtual asets to other users.
